      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p><span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your main source of energy. It comes from the foods you eat. A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells to give them energy. If you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use insulin well. The glucose then stays in your blood and not enough goes into your cells.</p><p>Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause health problems. But you can take steps to manage your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> and try to prevent these health problems.</p>What causes <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p><span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> may be caused by a combination of factors:</p><ul><li>Being overweight or having obesity</li><li>Not being physically active</li><li>Genetics and family history</li></ul><p><span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> usually starts with insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your cells don't respond normally to insulin. As a result, your body needs more insulin to help the glucose enter your cells. At first, your body makes more insulin to try to get cells to respond. But over time, your body can't make enough insulin, and your blood glucose levels rise.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>You are at higher risk of developing <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> if you:</p><ul><li>Are over age 45. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, but it is more common in middle-aged and older people.</li><li>Have prediabetes, which means that your blood glucose is high for you but not high enough to be called <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span></li><li>Had <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> in pregnancy or gave birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.</li><li>Have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span></li><li>Are overweight or have obesity</li><li>Are Black or African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, or Pacific Islander</li><li>Are not physically active</li><li>Have other conditions such as high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or depression</li><li>Have low HDL (good) cholesterol and high triglycerides</li><li>Have acanthosis nigricans - dark, thick, and velvety skin around your neck or armpits</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>Many people with <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> have no symptoms at all. If you do have them, the symptoms develop slowly over several years. They might be so mild that you do not notice them. The symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Increased thirst and urination</li><li>Increased hunger</li><li>Feeling tired</li><li>Blurred vision</li><li>Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands</li><li>Sores that do not heal</li><li>Unexplained weight loss</li></ul>How is <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Your provider will use blood tests to diagnose <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. The blood tests include:</p><ul><li>A1C test, which measures your average blood glucose level over the past 3 months.</li><li>Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) test, which measures your current blood glucose level. You need to fast (not eat or drink anything except water) for at least 8 hours before the test.</li><li>Random plasma glucose (RPG) test, which measures your current blood glucose level. This test is used when you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> symptoms and the provider does not want to wait for you to fast before having the test.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> involves managing your blood glucose levels. Many people are able to do this by living a healthy lifestyle. Some people may also need to take medicine:</p><ul><li>A healthy lifestyle includes following a healthy eating plan and getting regular physical activity. You need to learn how to balance what you eat and drink with physical activity and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> medicine, if you take any.</li><li>Medicines for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> include oral medicines, insulin, and other injectable medicines. Over time, some people will need to take more than one <span class="qt3">type</span> of medicine to control their <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</li><li>You will need to check your blood glucose regularly. Your provider will tell you how often you need to do it.</li><li>It's also important to keep your blood pressure and cholesterol levels close to the targets your provider sets for you. Make sure to get your screening tests regularly.</li></ul>Can <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> be prevented?<p>You can take steps to help prevent or delay <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> by losing weight if you are overweight, eating fewer calories, and being more physically active. If you have a condition which raises your risk for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, managing that condition may lower your risk of getting <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span> and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Children and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span></content>

      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Until recently, the common <span class="qt3">type</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> in children and teens was <span class="qt3">type</span> 1. It was called juvenile <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. With <span class="qt3">Type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, the pancreas does not make insulin. Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose,or sugar, get into your cells to give them energy. Without insulin, too much sugar stays in the blood.</p><p>Now younger people are also getting <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.  <span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> used to be called adult-onset <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. But now it is becoming more common in children and teens, due to more obesity. With <span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, the body does not make or use insulin well.</p><p>Children have a higher risk of <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> if they  are overweight or have obesity, have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, or are not active. Children who are African American, Hispanic, Native American/Alaska Native, Asian American, or Pacific Islander also have a higher risk. To lower the risk of <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> in children:</p><ul><li>Have them maintain a healthy weight</li><li>Be sure they are physically active</li><li>Have them eat smaller portions of healthy foods</li><li>Limit time with the TV, computer, and video</li></ul><p>Children and teens with <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> may need to take insulin. <span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> may be  controlled with diet and exercise. If not, patients will need to take oral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> medicines or insulin. A blood test called the A1C can check on how you are managing your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/howtopreventdiabetes.html">
      <content name="title">How to Prevent <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span> Prevention</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span>, also called <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes mellitus</span></span>, is a disease that causes your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels to be too high. There are three <span class="qt3">types</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>: <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, and <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. <span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> is the most common <span class="qt3">type</span> and may be prevented, delayed, or managed by making lifestyle changes.</p>What is <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>If you have <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use it well. This is called insulin resistance. Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose get into your cells. Glucose is your cells' main source of energy and comes from the foods you eat. If your body is resistant to insulin, then insulin can't get enough glucose into your cells. This then leads to glucose staying in your blood, leading to high blood glucose levels.</p><p>Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause health problems. If you are at risk for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, you might be able to prevent or delay developing it.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>Many people are at risk for <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. Your chances of getting it depend on a combination of risk factors such as your genes and lifestyle. The risk factors include:</p><ul><li>Having prediabetes, which means you have blood glucose levels that are high for you, but not high enough to be called <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span></li><li>Being overweight or having obesity</li><li>Being age 35 or older</li><li>A family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span></li><li>Being African American, Alaska Native, American Indian, Asian American, Hispanic/Latino, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander</li><li>Having high blood pressure</li><li>Having a low level of HDL (good) cholesterol or a high level of triglycerides</li><li>A history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> in pregnancy</li><li>Having given birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more</li><li>An inactive lifestyle</li><li>A history of heart disease or stroke</li><li>Having depression</li><li>Having polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)</li><li>Having acanthosis nigricans, a skin condition in which your skin becomes dark and thick, especially around your neck or armpits</li><li>Smoking</li></ul>How can I prevent or delay getting <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>Most of the things that you need to do to prevent or delay getting <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> involve having a healthier lifestyle. Lifestyle changes include:</p><ul><li>Lose weight.Weight control is an important part of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> prevention. You may be able to prevent or delay <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> by losing 5 to 7% of your current weight. For example, if you weigh 200 pounds, your goal would be to lose between 10 to 14 pounds. And once you lose the weight, it is important that you don't gain it back.</li><li>Follow a healthy eating plan. It is important to reduce the amount of calories you eat and drink each day, so you can lose weight and keep it off. To do that, your diet should include smaller portions and less fat and sugar. You should also eat a variety of foods from each food group, including plenty of whole grains, fruits, and vegetables. It's also a good idea to limit red meat and avoid processed meats.</li><li>Get regular exercise. Being physically active has many health benefits, including helping you to lose weight and lower your blood glucose levels. These both lower your risk of <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. Try to get at least 30 minutes of physical activity on most days of the week. The amount of exercise you need depends on your age and health. Even small amounts of exercise can be helpful. If you have not been active, talk with your health care provider to figure out which <span class="qt3">types</span> of exercise are best for you. You can start slowly and work up to your goal.</li><li>Don't smoke. Smoking can contribute to insulin resistance, which can lead to <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. If you already smoke, try to quit.</li><li>Talk to your provider to see whether there is anything else you can do to delay or to prevent <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. If you are at high risk, your provider may suggest that you take one of a few <span class="qt3">types</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> medicines.</li></ul><p>If you make these changes, you will get other health benefits as well. You may lower your risk of other diseases, and you will probably feel better and have more energy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span> and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span>, also known as <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes mellitus</span></span>, is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your body's main source of energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas. Insulin helps move glucose from your bloodstream into your cells, where it can be used for energy.</p><p>If you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body can't make insulin, can't use insulin as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. This can cause glucose levels to get too high. Over time, high blood glucose levels can lead to serious health conditions. But you can take steps to manage your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> and try to prevent these health problems.</p>What are the <span class="qt3">types</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>There are different <span class="qt3">types</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>:</p><ul><li><span class="qt3">Type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. If you have <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body makes little or no insulin. It happens when your immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin. </li><li><span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. This is the most common form of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. If you have <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body may still be able to make insulin, but your cells don't respond well to insulin. They can't easily take up enough glucose from your blood.</li><li>Gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. This is a form of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> that develops during pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>The different <span class="qt3">types</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> have different causes:</p><ul><li>Researchers think <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> is caused by genes and factors in the environment that might trigger the disease.</li><li><span class="qt3">Type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> is caused by several factors, including lifestyle factors and genes. The lifestyle factors include not being physically active and being overweight or having obesity.</li><li>Researchers think gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> is caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy along with genetic and lifestyle factors.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>The different <span class="qt3">types</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> have different risk factors:</p><ul><li>You can develop <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> at any age, but it most often starts in childhood. Having a parent or sibling with <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> may increase your chance of developing it.</li><li>You are at higher risk of developing <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> if you:</li><ul><li>Are overweight or have obesity.</li><li>Are over age 35. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, but it is more common in middle-aged and older adults.</li><li>Have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</li><li>Have prediabetes. This means that your blood glucose is higher than normal, but it's not high enough to be called <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</li><li>Had gestational <span Pacific Islander.</li><li>Are not physically active.</li><li>Have certain other health conditions, such as high blood pressure or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li></ul><li>You are at higher risk of developing gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> if you:</li><ul><li>Are overweight or have obesity.</li><li>Have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span more.</li><li>Have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li><li>Are African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander.</li></ul></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling very thirsty</li><li>Feeling very hungry</li><li>Urinating (peeing) more often, including at night</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Blurry vision</li><li>Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands</li><li>Sores that do not heal</li><li>Losing weight without trying</li></ul><p>But it's important to know that your symptoms may vary, depending on which <span class="qt3">type</span> you have:</p><ul><li>The symptoms of <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> usually come on quickly and can be severe.</li><li>With <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, the symptoms often develop slowly, over several years. The symptoms can be so mild that you might not even notice them.</li><li>Gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> often has no symptoms. If you do have symptoms, they may be mild. If you are pregnant, you will usually be screened for this condition between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. </li></ul>How is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your health care provider will use one or more glucose blood tests. There are several <span class="qt3">types</span>, including the A1C test.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> involves managing your blood glucose levels:</p><ul><li>If you have <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, you will need to take daily doses of insulin, either by injection or through a special pump. Some people also need to take another <span class="qt3">type</span> of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> medicine that works with insulin.</li><li>If you have <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, you may be able to manage or even reverse it by making lifestyle changes. These include eating a healthy diet, staying at healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity. Some people also need to take <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> medicines to manage their <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</li><li>If you have gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, you may be able to lower your glucose levels by eating a healthy diet and getting regular exercise. But be sure to talk to your provider about your treatment options. Gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> usually goes away after you give birth. But you will have a higher risk of developing <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> later.</li></ul><p>Checking your blood glucose levels is also an important part of managing your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. Ask your provider about the best way to check your blood glucose level and how often you should check it.</p>Can <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> be prevented?<p><span class="qt3">Type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> can't be prevented.</p><p>You may be able to delay or prevent <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> through the same lifestyle changes that are used to manage <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> (eating a healthy diet, staying at a healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity). These lifestyle changes may also help prevent gestational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span> and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>If you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose comes from foods you eat. The cells of your body need glucose for energy. A hormone called insulin helps glucose get into your cells.</p><p>With <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body doesn't make insulin. With <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, your body doesn't make or use insulin well. Without enough insulin, glucose builds up in your blood and causes high blood glucose levels.</p><p>Prediabetes means that your blood glucose levels are higher than normal but not high enough to be called <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>. If you have prediabetes, you are more likely to develop <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</p>How do the foods I eat affect my blood glucose levels?<p>The glucose in your blood comes from certain foods called carbohydrates, or "carbs." Foods that are high in carbs include candy and sweets, sodas, breads, tortillas, and white rice. The more carbs you eat, the higher your blood glucose level will be. Some, but not all people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, may need to count the amount of carbs eaten in drinks and meals.</p><p>Whether you have <span class="qt3">type</span> 1 or <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, making the right food choices is an important way to keep your blood glucose at a level that is healthy for you. When you control your blood glucose, you lower your chance of having serious health problems from <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, such as vision loss and heart problems.</p><p>And if you have prediabetes or are at risk for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, eating foods that keep your blood glucose levels healthy may help prevent <span class="qt3">type</span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">2</span></span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> later on.</p>What's the best diet for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>There isn't a specific diet or meal plan that works for everybody. Your health care provider may have you see a registered dietician (RD) or a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> educator who can help design the best eating plan for you. The plan will consider:</p><ul><li>Any medicines that you take</li><li>Your weight</li><li>Any other health conditions you have</li><li>Your lifestyle and tastes</li><li>Your goals</li></ul><p>All eating plans for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> have a few things in common, including eating the right foods in the right amounts at the right times.</p>What foods should I eat if I have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>?<p>Eating the right foods for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span> means eating a variety of healthy foods from all the food groups:</p><ul><li>Fruits and vegetables</li><li>Whole grains, such as whole wheat, brown rice, barley, quinoa, and oats</li><li>Proteins, such as lean meats, chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, nuts, beans, lentils, and tofu</li><li>Nonfat or low-fat dairy, such as milk, yogurt, and cheese</li></ul>What foods should I limit to control my blood glucose?<p>To keep your blood glucose under control, you may need to cut back on certain foods and drinks. This doesn't mean that you can never enjoy them. But you should have them less often or in smaller amounts.</p><p>The foods and drinks you should limit include:</p><ul><li>High-carb foods and drinks, such as:
	<ul><li>Sugary foods, such as candy, cookies, cake, ice cream, sweetened cereals, and canned fruits with added sugar</li><li>Drinks with added sugars, such as juice, regular soda, and regular sports or energy drinks</li><li>White rice, tortillas, breads, and pasta - especially those made with white flour</li><li>Starchy vegetables, such as white potatoes, corn, and peas</li></ul></li><li>Fried foods and other foods high in saturated and trans fats.</li><li>Foods high in sodium (salt).</li><li>Alcohol. If you do drink, you should drink moderately. This means no more than one standard drink a day if you're a woman or <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">two</span></span> standard drinks a day if you're a man.</li></ul>What else do I need to know about diabetic diets?<p>If you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>, it's important to eat the right amount of food every day. Your eating plan will include how much to eat, and help you choose the <span class="qt3">types</span> of food for each meal or snack. If you take insulin, you may need to learn how to count carbs to help you know how much insulin to take.</p><p>Eating at the right times is also important. You will want to plan for regular, balanced meals to avoid blood glucose levels that are too high or too low for you. Eating about the same amount of carbs at each meal can be helpful.</p><p>Your eating plan will also teach you how to stick with your plan at home and when you eat out.</p><p>Eating healthy to control your blood glucose does take some effort. But the reward is a chance to live your healthiest life with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">diabetes</span></span>.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Diabetes</span></span> and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
